title: The lowest seat (Luke 14:1–14)
hook: don't take the top place; invite those who can't repay you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod the fox and Jesus like a mother hen, wings open over Jerusalem. Your line was under her wings. Did you send the invitation? Day five hundred fifty-four.

A wedding reception. You walk in, and there's no seating plan. Near the head table, a few empty chairs. At the back, by the kitchen door, a table where nobody seems to know anybody. Where do you sit? In Jesus' world this mattered even more. At a formal meal, where you reclined showed everyone how important you were. Luke says Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, and he watches the guests come in. He notices how they choose the best places. And then, being Jesus, he says so.
screen: `WHERE YOU SIT SHOWS WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: His advice starts out sounding like ordinary good manners. Don't grab the top place; someone more honored might arrive, and the host will ask you to move, and you'll walk the whole room to the bottom with everyone watching. Instead, in the King James Bible: "go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher." Room there means place, a seat at the table. This wasn't new wisdom. The book of Proverbs says nearly the same thing: don't push yourself forward before the king, because it's better to be told come up here than to be put lower. Jesus is drawing on his own people's old wisdom. But then he lifts it into something bigger: "For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." That's not seating strategy anymore. It's how the kingdom of God works. The ones who push up end up down; the ones who go low are called higher. And then he turns to the host, and it gets more uncomfortable. When you give a dinner, don't just invite friends, family and rich neighbors, who'll invite you back. "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee." The whole social system of the dinner party ran on return invitations. He asks for a guest list made of people who can't pay you back. The repayment, he says, comes later, at the resurrection of the just. Lowest seat for the guest. Open door for the host. Both are about letting go of the score.

Here's the practice: invite someone who can't repay. Settle and breathe. Run through the people you usually share meals or time with. Notice how many of them return the favor; that's normal and good. Now widen the circle. Who do you know, or pass, who rarely gets invited anywhere? An older neighbor living alone. A new coworker. Someone going through a hard time with nothing to offer back. Picture setting a place for them. Then choose one, and decide how you'll invite them: coffee, a meal, a seat at your table. If you pray, you can ask for open doors. The bell holds the time.
The lowest seat. Jesus' advice at a dinner: take the low place, let the host call you higher, and fill your table with those who can't repay.
Your line: friend, go up higher. Today, take the less important seat, the slower line, the last turn, and let someone else go first. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Many churches and Christian groups run community meals and soup kitchens open to anyone, and some Christians make a habit of inviting people who are often left out to their own tables, especially at holidays.

original.note: Greek: last, lowest. the lowest place at the table; the same word gives us eschatology, the study of last things.

trapdoor: what you thought: good table manners.
what it means: the kingdom reverses rank: go low and be called higher, and fill your table with people who can't repay.
what a scholar hears: Jesus draws on Proverbs 25, then lifts it into a rule of the kingdom and challenges a dinner culture built on return invitations.
